accroche: The doctor is named Frankenstein. His creature never had a name, until a 1927 stage play.
contenu_vulgarise:
Ask anyone to describe Frankenstein: a green giant with a square skull and two bolts in his neck. Almost no one will say that he is a young scientist from Geneva. For nearly a century, the creator's name has slid onto his creature, and Mary Shelley's novel, published in 1818, has nothing to do with it.

## What the Text Really Says

In *Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus*, the creature is never named. Victor Frankenstein, who assembles him and then abandons him on the very first night, refers to him by a series of epithets that express his disgust: “monster,” “dæmon,” “devil,” “wretch.” The creature himself, when he addresses his creator, compares himself to Adam, a heavily loaded biblical reference: Adam, for his part, had a God who recognized him and named him. He has nothing of the kind; he says instead that he is the fallen angel, driven from joy without having committed any fault. This silence about the name is not an oversight on the author's part: it is the knot of the novel. For Victor, to refuse to name his creation is to refuse to be its father.

## Where the Confusion Comes From

The error has a precise date and origin. In December 1927, in Preston, a stage adaptation written by Peggy Webling is mounted by the producer Hamilton Deane. For the first time, the play calls the creature “Frankenstein,” like his creator, a theatrical shortcut that simplifies the poster and the plot. The play tours for two years with *Dracula* before reaching London in 1930. The following year, Universal draws on it for the script of its film with Boris Karloff: the name sticks to the creature, the image of the square face and the bolts takes hold in the movies, and the confusion, already begun on stage, is fixed for good in popular culture.

## A Misreading That, in Spite of Itself, Gets It Right

One could stop there: a mix-up of titles, without consequence. But it replays, unknowingly, the very argument of the novel. Shelley never separated the scientist from his creature by accident: she wanted to show that a creator cannot wash his hands of what he makes, even, especially, when he refuses to name it. By merging the two under a single name, popular culture erased the exact detail of the text, but it has, almost in spite of itself, made visible what Victor Frankenstein spends the entire novel denying: he and his creature are one.

repere.texte: It is a 1927 stage adaptation, written by Peggy Webling and first performed in Preston in December of that year, that invents calling the creature “Frankenstein,” a century after the novel's publication.

carte.punch: The doctor is named Frankenstein. His creature never had a name in the novel.

quiz.question: Why did the scientist's name end up designating the creature in popular culture?
choix: Because Mary Shelley names the creature “Frankenstein” in the novel's last chapter
Because a 1927 stage adaptation was the first to give the creature that name
Because 19th-century French translators confused the two characters
Because Boris Karloff chose that name for his role in the 1931 film
quiz.explication: The 1818 novel never names the creature. It is Peggy Webling's play, staged in 1927, that invents this theatrical shortcut; the 1931 Universal film, drawing on it, then popularizes it worldwide. Neither the translators nor Karloff are at its origin: the actor merely inherited a name already fixed by the stage.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the creature compare himself to Adam, in the novel?
choix: He says he is rather the fallen angel, driven from joy without having committed any fault
He claims to be a perfect Adam, loved without reservation by his creator
He rejects any biblical comparison and calls himself a purely scientific creation
He compares himself to Adam because Victor Frankenstein named him that
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The creature notes that Adam had a God who recognized him and named him; lacking that, he says he is rather the fallen angel, driven from joy without having committed any fault.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what year does Mary Shelley publish Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mary Shelley's novel is published in 1818, nearly a century before the 1927 play renamed the creature with his creator's name.

The director James Whale, who would later shoot the 1931 film
The actress Peggy Webling herself, in the lead role
The novelist Bram Stoker, author of Dracula
